summary: The first live bench of myidsan's brute-force lockout against a real two-instance CLUSTER (two myidsan containers on one shared Postgres and one shared Redis, the shipped configuration) found and fixed two real defects. First, the failed-login lockout (domain/shared/apis.LoginGuard) was purely per-process, so on a clustered deployment - myidsan is documented as genuinely clusterable, and has a wizard step and a Settings panel for declaring it - an attacker's effective budget was maxAttempts times the instance count, and a user locked out on one instance could simply be routed to another and sign in: the bench watched instance A lock an account after eight wrong passwords, then instance B evaluate a ninth normally and go on to accept the CORRECT password with 200. Fixed with a new LoginGuard.WithSharedStore(store, namespace), which mirrors lockout state into the shared cache alongside the existing in-memory map rather than replacing it - a locked verdict is the OR of the two, so the shared half can only ever lock more, never less, and an unreachable cache degrades the guard to exactly today's per-process behaviour rather than disabling brute-force protection. Wired in apps/myidsan/app/app.go whenever cache.provider is redis/redis-cluster. Second, three authenticated endpoints that re-check the signed-in caller's own password had no throttle at all, making each a password oracle for anyone holding a stolen session cookie: POST /api/login/default/change-password (worst - a correct guess there replaces the password and takes the account permanently), DELETE /api/mfa/webauthn/{id} (its identity re-proof accepts the password alone, no second factor required), and DELETE /api/mfa (defence in depth only, since its code gate already fires first). All three now go through new selfThrottleLocked/selfThrottleFailure helpers keyed on the session's own account, so a stranger cannot aim the counter at somebody else. Also fixed along the way: infra/cache.MemoryStore.Delete did not clear a key's sliding-window rate-limit state (kept in a separate map from the cached value), so it meant something different there than on Redis, where the window IS the key - found because the lockout clears a key exactly that way on a successful sign-in.
compatibility: Backward-compatible; no migration needed. Single-instance installs and installs on a non-shared cache provider are completely unaffected - WithSharedStore is only attached when cache.provider is redis/redis-cluster, and even then the in-memory guard keeps working exactly as before as the fallback half. A clustered myidsan deployment on Redis now gets deployment-wide lockout enforcement automatically on upgrade, with no configuration change - the existing loginSecurity thresholds apply across the whole deployment instead of per instance. A correct password/code from a legitimate, non-attacking user behaves identically to before on every surface. Known and deliberate limit, pinned by a test: a success on one instance clears the shared counter but cannot clear another instance's in-memory tally, so a narrow sequence (fail almost-to-threshold on A, succeed on B, fail once more on A) can still trip a lockout on A alone - bounded to one base lockout, and the failure mode errs toward locking rather than admitting an attacker. myseliasan, the suite's other Tier A clusterable app, is unchanged - its LoginGuard is not yet wired to a shared store, since no bench covers its login surfaces.
